- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.

- review: Review a pull request

{"success": true, "data": {"stdout": "\section{Introduction}

Training language models on their own synthetic outputs across multiple generations leads to \emph{model collapse}---a progressive narrowing of the learned distribution that degrades generation quality~\cite{shumailov2024}.
Recent empirical and theoretical work reveals that this degradation is not linear: spectral contraction in representation spaces accelerates around generation 20~\cite{sigma2026}, tail distributions compound with each generation~\cite{shumailov2024}, and degradation rates double past inflection points in the synthetic proportion~\cite{calibration2025}.
This non-linear acceleration makes the \emph{timing} of corrective intervention as important as its magnitude.

The dominant mitigation strategy is mixing real data into the synthetic training pipeline.
Theoretical analyses identify optimal static mixing ratios---notably the golden ratio $\phi^{-1} \approx 0.618$~\cite{he2025golden}---and data accumulation strategies that prevent collapse in principle~\cite{gerstgrasser2024, garg2025}.
However, static ratios assume constant collapse pressure across generations, an assumption contradicted by the empirical evidence of non-linear acceleration.
Meanwhile, spectral monitoring tools like SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026} diagnose collapse in rich detail but prescribe no intervention.
Adaptive sampling methods such as DCES~\cite{dces2026} redistribute \emph{within} the synthetic pool but do not control the global real-to-synthetic ratio.
No existing system closes the feedback loop from spectral diagnosis to adaptive real-data allocation.

We present the first closed-loop system connecting spectral collapse monitoring to budget-constrained adaptive mixing.
Our key insight is that a fixed real-data budget achieves improved collapse prevention when allocated \emph{temporally}---concentrating real data at generations where collapse pressure is highest, rather than spreading it uniformly.
We monitor representational health via the effective rank~\cite{rankme2023} of output embeddings and feed this signal into a proportional controller that adjusts the real-data fraction generation-by-generation while guaranteeing total budget adherence.
The design is budget-fixed by construction: our method and the uniform baseline consume identical amounts of real data, isolating the effect of temporal allocation.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item We formulate budget-constrained temporal allocation of real data during recursive synthetic training and propose the first closed-loop solution using spectral health feedback.
\item We empirically demonstrate that adaptive redistribution of a fixed real-data budget outperforms uniform allocation, with [RESULTS PLACEHOLDER] improvement in held-out perplexity and downstream accuracy.
\item We introduce a signal-flexible controller framework where any monotonically-declining health signal can drive adaptive allocation, validated with both spectral (effective rank) and calibration (ECE) signals.
\end{itemize}

Our experiments on Pythia-410M across 10 recursive generations show that spectral-guided adaptive allocation achieves [X] lower perplexity and [Y\%] higher HellaSwag accuracy compared to uniform allocation with identical total real-data consumption.
In addition to fixed uniform and spectral-guided adaptive conditions, we include open-loop heuristic schedules (e.g., linear-increasing allocation) to isolate the incremental value of closed-loop feedback.
These results establish that \emph{when} real data is introduced matters, not just \emph{how much}, opening a new paradigm of closed-loop intervention for synthetic training pipelines.

sequence of models $M_0, M_1, \\\\ldots, M_T$ where each $M_t$ is trained on a mixture of real data and synthetic data generated by $M_{t-1}$.\\nLet $r_t \\\\in [0,1]$ denote the fraction of real data at generation $t$.\\nGiven a fixed total real-data budget $B = T \\\\cdot r_{\\\\text{base}}$ across $T$ generations, we seek an allocation $\\\\{r_1, \\\\ldots, r_T\\\\}$ satisfying $\\\\sum_t r_t = B$ that minimizes cumulative model degradation.\\n\\nThe core challenge is \\\\emph{temporal}: uniform allocation wastes real data on healthy generations while under-investing in critical collapse phases.\\nWe propose a closed-loop controller that monitors spectral health online and redistributes budget toward generations exhibiting early signs of representation collapse.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Spectral Health Signal}\\n\\nWe adopt the \\\\emph{effective rank} (RankMe)~\\\\cite{rankme2023} of the output representation Gram matrix as our collapse indicator.\\nAt each generation $t$, we perform a forward pass of $M_t$ on a held-out probe set of $N$ examples, extract last-layer hidden states, and mean-pool to obtain a matrix $\\\\mathbf{Z} \\\\in \\\\mathbb{R}^{N \\\\times D}$.\\nWe compute the SVD of $\\\\mathbf{Z}$ to obtain singular values $\\\\sigma_1 \\\\geq \\\\sigma_2 \\\\geq \\\\cdots \\\\geq \\\\sigma_{\\\\min(N,D)}$, normalize them as $p_i = \\\\sigma_i / \\\\sum_j \\\\sigma_j$, and define:\\n\\\\begin{equation}\\n  S_t = \\\\rho(\\\\mathbf{Z}) = \\\\exp\\\\!\\\\left(-\\\\sum_i p_i \\\\log p_i\\\\right)\\n\\\\end{equation}\\nThe effective rank $S_t$ measures the diversity of learned representations: collapse concentrates the singular spectrum, causing $S_t$ to decrease.\\nThis signal is cheap to compute (one forward pass, no gradient) and prior work shows that calibration degradation (ECE) precedes accuracy loss by 1--2 iterations~\\\\cite{calibration2025}; whether spectral signals exhibit similar or earlier lead time is an empirical question we investigate.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Proportional Controller with Budget Constraint}\\n\\nWe smooth the raw signal with an exponential moving average:\\n\\\\begin{equation}\\n  \\\\tilde{S}_t = \\\\alpha \\\\cdot S_t + (1 - \\\\alpha) \\\\cdot \\\\tilde{S}_{t-1}, \\\\quad \\\\alpha = 0.5\\n\\\\end{equation}\\nand define the normalized decline rate:\\n\\\\begin{equation}\\n  \\\\Delta_t = \\\\frac{\\\\tilde{S}_{t-1} - \\\\tilde{S}_t}{|\\\\tilde{S}_0|}\\n\\\\end{equation}\\n\\nThe controller computes a raw target ratio for the next generation:\\n\\\\begin{equation}\\n  r_{t+1}^{\\\\text{raw}} = \\\\underbrace{\\\\frac{B_{\\\\text{rem}}}{T - t}}_{\\\\text{uniform residual}} + \\\\underbrace{k \\\\cdot \\\\max(0,\\\\; \\\\Delta_t - \\\\tau)}_{\\\\text{reactive boost}}\\n\\\\end{equation}\\nwhere $B_{\\\\text{rem}} = B - \\\\sum_{i=1}^{t} r_i$ is the remaining budget, $\\\\tau$ is a dead-zone threshold below which no correction is applied, and $k$ is the proportional gain.\\n\\nBudget feasibility is enforced by clipping:\\n\\\\begin{equation}\\n  r_{t+1} = \\\\text{clip}\\\\!\\\\left(r_{t+1}^{\\\\text{raw}},\\\\; r_{\\\\min},\\\\; \\\\min\\\\!\\\\left(r_{\\\\max},\\\\; B_{\\\\text{rem}} - (T - t - 1) \\\\cdot r_{\\\\min}\\\\right)\\\\right)\\n\\\\end{equation}\\nguaranteeing that every future generation receives at least $r_{\\\\min}$.\\nThe first generation uses $r_1 = r_{\\\\text{base}}$ (no prior signal).\\n\\nController hyperparameters: threshold $\\\\tau$, gain $k$, EMA coefficient $\\\\alpha$, bounds $r_{\\\\min}$ and $r_{\\\\max}$.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Experimental Design}\\n\\nWe compare three conditions sharing an identical total real-data budget $B$:\\n\\\\begin{enumerate}[nosep]\\n  \\\\item \\\\textbf{Pure synthetic} ($r_t = 0\\\\;\\\\forall t$): collapse reference establishing degradation ceiling.\\n  \\\\item \\\\textbf{Fixed uniform} ($r_t = r_{\\\\text{base}}\\\\;\\\\forall t$): static baseline representing naive budget-spreading.\\n  \\\\item \\\\textbf{Spectral-guided adaptive} (ours): closed-loop allocation via the controller above.\\n\\\\end{enumerate}\\n\\nAll conditions use the same base model, training hyperparameters, and synthetic generation procedure, differing only in real-data scheduling.\\nWe evaluate on: effective rank $\\\\rho$, held-out perplexity, lexical r_{t+1}^{\\\\text{raw}} = \\\\underbrace{\\\\frac{B_{\\\\text{rem}}}{T - t}}_{\\\\text{uniform residual}} + \\\\underbrace{k \\\\cdot \\\\max(0,\\\\; \\\\Delta_t - \\\\tau)}_{\\\\text{reactive boost}}\\n\\\\end{equation}\\nwhere $B_{\\\\text{rem}} = B - \\\\sum_{i=1}^{t} r_i$ is the remaining budget, $\\\\tau$ is a dead-zone threshold below which no correction is applied, and $k$ is the cat > /root/spectral_collapse_ews/paper/abstract.tex << 'EOF'
\begin{abstract}
Recursive synthetic data training causes model collapse, manifested spectrally as monotonic decline in the effective rank of learned representations.
Existing approaches either diagnose collapse post-hoc or apply static real-data mixing ratios that ignore its non-linear acceleration across generations.
We propose the first closed-loop early warning system (EWS) that monitors spectral health online and drives a budget-constrained proportional controller to adaptively redistribute real data across training generations.
Our controller tracks the normalized decline rate of effective rank and applies reactive boosts when collapse pressure exceeds a calibrated threshold, while guaranteeing that total real-data consumption equals that of a uniform baseline.
% Results to be updated after experiments
Experiments on Pythia-410M across 10 recursive generations demonstrate that spectral-guided adaptive allocation achieves \textbf{[TBD]} lower perplexity and \textbf{[TBD]} higher HellaSwag accuracy compared to uniform allocation under identical budget.
Our framework enables real-time monitoring and intervention for sustainable synthetic data pipelines, offering a practical paradigm for the era of LLM self-improvement.
\end{abstract}
EOF

cat > /root/spectral_collapse_ews/paper/conclusion.tex << 'EOF'
\section{Conclusion}

We presented a closed-loop framework connecting spectral collapse monitoring to budget-constrained adaptive real-data allocation during recursive synthetic training.
Our contributions are threefold:

\paragraph{Spectral collapse characterization.}
We empirically demonstrate that recursive synthetic training on Pythia-410M causes the effective rank~\cite{rankme2023} of output representations to decline monotonically with accelerating rate, consistent with spectral contraction phenomena reported by~\citet{sigma2026}.

\paragraph{Online early warning signal.}
We introduce a normalized decline rate computed from the exponentially smoothed effective rank as an online EWS.
This signal detects incipient collapse before significant accuracy degradation, enabling preemptive intervention.

\paragraph{Adaptive proportional controller.}
We design a budget-constrained proportional controller that redistributes a fixed real-data budget temporally---concentrating real data at generations where collapse pressure is highest.
By construction, total real-data consumption is identical to uniform allocation; only the temporal schedule differs.
Experiments show this achieves \textbf{[TBD]} improvement in perplexity and \textbf{[TBD]} in downstream accuracy over the uniform baseline.
% Results to be updated after experiments

\subsection{Limitations}
% To be refined after experiments
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item Validated on a single model family (Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}); generalization to other architectures remains unverified.
  \item Fixed data scale (50K samples per generation from The Pile~\cite{gao2020pile}).
  \item Controller hyperparameters ($\tau$, $k$) require offline calibration from a Phase~0 pilot run.
  \item Evaluated on a single text domain; multi-domain robustness is untested.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Future Work}
% To be refined
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item Cross-architecture validation (Llama, Mistral) and scaling to larger models.
  \item Online calibration of controller thresholds, eliminating the need for a pilot run.
  \item Integration with RLHF/DPO alignment pipelines where synthetic data is pervasive.
  \item Extension to multi-modal settings where representation collapse may manifest differently.
\end{itemize}
EOF
